LESSON MENU
THEORY OF OPERATION
There are many different methods of controlling motors by using feedback to indicate speed. Input DC Output Motor Feedback Circuit Feedback Control
DISCUSSION
Closed loop feedback systems are recognized by the fact that there is a "closed loop" from motor output to motor input.
The Nida 280 trainer and 130 test console can be configured as a closed loop feedback system. 280 130
The Nida experiment card PC130-281 contains the controlling circuitry.
Let's examine the closed loop feedback system used on the 280 trainer. 280 Input DC Output Motor Feedback Circuit
The DC motor receives it's input power from the PC130-281 by way of the PC130-280 card.
The variac supplies 360 sinewave power to PC130-281 where it is applied to a 360 triac controller.
The Triac controller in PC130-281 is controlled by the RPM output of the 280 trainer, a closed loop system.
Motor output shaft RPM is detected by means of a magnetic pickup.
Motor shaft RPM information is fed to the motor controlling circuitry.
The signal is then processed and fed back to the DC motor as an input signal.
Which of the following detects motor shaft RPM?
The controlling circuitry receives the shaft RPM information but does not detect shaft RPM.
TRY AGAIN!
The DC motor produces shaft RPM and receives input signals from the controlling circuitry.
TRY AGAIN!
The magnetic pickup used on the 280 trainer generates an RPM sensitive signal.
The teeth of the output shaft create ON and OFF spots that are detected by the pickup.
This signal is sent to the interface card for digital processing (IC1). The signal is converted to a square wave.
Now, let's see how the feedback circuit on PC130-281 operates.
The square wave signal, indicating motor speed, is then sent to the DC motor control circuitry for further processing.
Q1 is a common emitter amplifier which applies a small gain to the signal while inverting it.
Q2 and Q3 form a monostable multivibrator circuit.
The multivibrator circuit produces a constant width signal with a frequency variation proportional to motor RPM. Constant width
This constant width signal is applied to IC1...............
IC1 and its associated components form a filter circuit that changes the variable frequency square wave into a proportional DC level.
Notice that the multivibrator signal is connected to the inverting input of the op-amp.
As the input signal frequency decreases, the DC output from the op-amp decreases. + VDC DC Signal 0 V
As the input signal frequency increases, the DC output from the op-amp increases.
The frequency variations are now directly related to DC amplitude variations.
IC2 inverts the signal again and R12 provides an adjustable negative bias as an offset.
In other words, the bias from R12 is overcome by the signal level from IC1. IC2 is the comparator circuit.
IC3 is an opto-isolator. This component insulates low voltage semiconductor circuits from high voltage AC circuits.
By having an optical (rather than physical) connection between the circuits, IC3 serves as a safe interface.
The signal from IC3 is applied to Q4 where it is amplified.
Triac Q5, zener diode D4, and D3 comprise the 360 time controller.
Notice that Q5 is in series to the 60 Hz input power.
The triac turns on when a gate voltage is applied, and the time controlling the power to the DC motor.
The gate voltage to Q5 is developed by IC2, the comparator.
For a constant RPM input, what signal is applied to the gate of Q5?
Applying 0 volts to the gate of Q5 would not allow Q5 to turn ON. In other words, no power applied to the motor and the rotation would stop.

5. Vary R12 on PC130-281 while observing the viewed waveform.
While varying R12, the viewed waveform _______ varied proportionally.
Varying the speed of the motor has no bearing on feedback signal amplitude or intensity. This signal is the magnetic pickup loop signal from PC130-280 and is frequency sensitive only.

9. Connect CH1 oscilloscope probe to TP3 on the PC130-281 card.
10. Vary R12 on PC130-281 while observing the viewed waveform.
Notice that as motor RPM increased, so did the DC voltage level.
TP3 is the DC output from IC1. A frequency change from the motor corresponds to a DC voltage level variation.
This frequency sensitive DC waveform is then fed into IC2 where it is amplified and given a negative bias.
IC3 and Q4 translate proportional voltage, to a time variable turn on signal, that is applied to the gate of triac, Q5.
11. Place the CH1 X10 oscilloscope probe on the control 1 TP of the 280 card. Use the control 2 TP for ground. 280 Rotating Machinery Interface Nida Corp.
12. Set the oscilloscope to 2ms Time/Div and 2 Volts/Div..
13. While observing the oscilloscope screen, turn R12 Motor Speed potentiometer fully CCW.
Notice that the output to the motor was reduced to zero or almost zero.
14. Now, rotate R12 almost fully CW (arrow pointing to the left) while again observing the oscilloscope.
You should have observed a stable sine wave until the motor reached the base speed where the sine wave began to flutter.
This is caused by the action of IC3 and Q4 switching the triac on and off to maintain a steady motor speed as compared to the base speed.
BASE SPEED = MOTOR SPEED
The RPM of the motor affected its input voltage, verifying Closed Loop Feedback Operation.
